To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the mutual information between a system input and its output can be decomposed into components characterizing the direct and indirect effects of that input, (b) the direct and indirect components can be further decomposed into components quantifying the main effects of individual inputs, and (c) the direct and the indirect components are additive, and therefore the mutual information can be decomposed in terms of the main effect components.

(1) we have developed a general method for quantifying the importance of each element that acts as a system input in determining the output; and (2) we have applied this methodology to a number of different systems, including the human visual system, to show how it provides new insight that is otherwise inaccessible.

(i) the sensitivity of a system output to an input can be decomposed into a series of components that quantify the main effect and all possible interactions of the input; (ii) the main effect and interaction components can be calculated by solving a set of linear equations; (iii) the method can be used to determine the relative importance of different system inputs and to identify those interactions that have the largest influence on the output(s).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a general framework for credit assignment in systems that can be represented as complex networks.
the development of a novel methodology for credit assignment in large complex networks, and its application to problems such as the design of optimal interventions in social and biological systems.
the question how to measure the influence of individual elements of complex networks on their collective dynamics, in particular, on their output.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the proposed method is a powerful and flexible tool for the analysis of complex networks and it has a wide range of potential applications.

the proposed method can be used to determine the sensitivity of any system to its inputs, and that the method is applicable to a very large class of systems, which includes many of the systems of interest in the natural and social sciences.
the information-theoretic sensitivity approach provides a powerful tool for the analysis of complex systems, which can be used in a wide range of applications.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
it provides a general framework for credit assignment in any complex network.
we propose a novel information-theoretic framework for sensitivity analysis in complex networks, which can be used for a wide range of problems.
we propose a general method to quantify the importance of inputs in complex networks.
The main takeaway from our work is that

information theory can provide a general framework for sensitivity analysis, and that the resulting measures of sensitivity have a direct physical interpretation in terms of the flow of information in the system.
information theory can serve as an alternative to traditional sensitivity analysis techniques for credit assignment in systems with complex interactions.
information theory provides an elegant and unified framework for sensitivity analysis of complex systems.
